qt: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Nikolas Farantouris (S&D) Subject:

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which was signed on 7 August 2026, is currently the most important diplomatic development in the Middle East, as it militarily ‘unites’ Türkiye, a country that works with the Euro-Atlantic institutions, with Pakistan, the only Muslim state in possession of nuclear weapons, and Saudi Arabia, the most powerful force in the Gulf. The agreement is worthy of special attention, as it signals an effort to pursue new and independent diplomatic action in the region. Although the exact content of the agreement has not been made public, certain key aspects have been made known, e.g. that it contains a mutual military assistance clause and promotes common military and industrial projects. However, many question marks remain. Despite these question marks, press reports have portrayed the Commission’s reaction to the agreement as ‘positive’1. In view of the above, can the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy answer the following: 1.
What is the Commission’s official stance on the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement?
What is the exact content and what are the expected consequences of the agreement, given the concerns it raises about its impact on the balance in the Eastern Mediterranean?
Are the clauses of the agreement in line with the EU’s new security and defence architecture?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.11.2026) The EU has taken note of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye on 7 August 20261. The Agreement has gained renewed attention in the context of the recent regional military escalation. The EU considers that regional security arrangements can contribute positively to stability and confidence-building, provided they respect international law and the principles of the UN Charter. This is also the case in the Eastern Mediterranean, where the EU remains committed to dialogue, de-escalation and regional stability, while firmly defending the interests of the EU and its Member States, in accordance with international law and the principle of goodneighbourly relations. In general, such regional arrangements should contribute to deescalation, regional stability and an inclusive and cooperative security environment. The security and stability of the Gulf and the broader Middle East are closely interconnected with European security and are of strategic importance to the EU. The EU will continue to engage closely with EU candidate country and NATO partner Türkiye, as well as with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and other regional partners to promote dialogue, conflict prevention and longterm regional stability. It will also deepen its growing security and defence cooperation with Gulf partners, in line with the EU’s security and defence objectives.
